assessment.title: Homework #3 · Diode circuits
assessment.topic: Module 3 · Diodes · Ideal and constant-drop models · Small-signal regulation
assessment.instructions: Show key steps, assumptions, and final answers with units. For every diode, state the assumed state and verify it (ON: i_D ≥ 0; OFF: v_D below the turn-on drop). Use the circuit workspace to draw or annotate the circuits; your working goes on the solution canvas. Enter numbers in the units shown. Practical task: predict first, build the schematic and breadboard yourself, check connections, test, and explain. Use Save progress in the homework toolbar, then reopen the downloaded JSON with Open saved homework. There is no homework file byte-size cap; available device memory and browser storage still apply. Keep a downloaded backup.

questions.title: 1) Ideal diodes: conduction state and node voltage
questions.promptHtml:
In each circuit (a), (b), and (c), node v is fed from +3 V and returns to ground through the elements shown. The diodes are ideal: a short circuit when ON and an open circuit when OFF.

  1. Determine whether each diode conducts.
  2. Find v and the current I.

Take I as the current flowing from the +3 V supply down toward ground (0 if no current flows).
hints: Assume a state, solve, then check: an ON diode needs i_D ≥ 0; an OFF diode needs v_D ≤ 0.
In (b) and (c), check which terminal of the diode is the anode.
checklist: State the assumed diode state for each circuit.
Verify it with i_D ≥ 0 or v_D ≤ 0.
Report v and I with units.

questions.title: 2(a) Two diodes, constant-drop model (R_top = 15 kΩ)
questions.promptHtml:
Silicon diodes, constant-voltage-drop model: VD ≈ 0.7 V when ON, open circuit when OFF. Circuit (a): +10 V → 15 kΩ → node V; D2 from V to node B; D1 from ground to B; B → 5 kΩ → −10 V.

  1. Determine which diode(s) are ON and which are OFF.
  2. Find the node voltage V (with respect to ground).
  3. Find I (through D1, downward) and ID2 (through D2, downward).
hints: Start by assuming both diodes ON: then B = −0.7 V and V = 0 V.
Check that the current into B through D₁ is positive.
checklist: Verify every ON current ≥ 0 and every OFF voltage ≤ 0.7 V.

questions.title: 3) Diode-string regulator: nominal point and line regulation
questions.promptHtml:
A 10 V supply feeds R = 1 kΩ into a string of three forward diodes to ground. The string provides vo ≈ 2.1 V at the nominal current.

  1. Find the nominal current in the diode string.
  2. Using the small-signal model, estimate the incremental resistance of one diode rd and of the string rd,string at the nominal current, with n = 1 and VT = 25 mV.
  3. Using small-signal analysis, compute the change in vo and its percentage for a ±1 V supply change.

The source sentence omits the ideality factor; n = 1 matches the course Walkthrough 4.
hints: r_d = nV_T/I_D for each diode; the three are in series.
The supply change divides between R and r_d,string.
checklist: Find I_D from the drop across R.
Compute r_d and the string resistance.
Apply the small-signal divider to Δv_S = ±1 V.

questions.title: 4) Load regulation of the diode-string regulator
questions.promptHtml:
For the regulator of Problem 3, a load RL = 1 kΩ is connected across vo.

  1. Find the new DC current through R.
  2. Estimate the new diode-string current and the new output voltage vo (small-signal model about the nominal point, n = 1, VT = 25 mV).
  3. Report vo for the no-load case.
hints: The load draws about v_o/R_L ≈ 2.1 mA, taken away from the diode string.
For a self-consistent value, write KCL at v_o with the string modeled as 2.1 V + r_d,string·Δi_D.
checklist: Find Δi_D and Δv_o with r_string.
Update I_R, I_D and v_o; compare with no load.

hints: The higher input wins: assume D_A ON and test D_B.
D_B is OFF if its anode is below its cathode + 0.7 V.

questions.promptHtml:
A silicon diode (n = 1, VT = 25 mV) is biased by a dc current ID = 0.5 mA. A small current change Δi = ±50 μA is superimposed.

questions.title: 7) Diode small-signal analysis: ac ripple on a dc supply
questions.promptHtml:
A 10 V dc supply with a superimposed ac ripple vs of 1 V peak feeds R = 10 kΩ in series with a silicon diode to ground. Use the constant-drop model (0.7 V) for the dc bias and the small-signal model with n = 1 and VT = 25 mV.

  1. Find the dc diode current ID.
  2. Find the small-signal resistance rd.
  3. Draw the small-signal equivalent circuit in the workspace (dc source → ac ground, diode → rd).
  4. Find the peak ac voltage vd across the diode and the peak ac diode current id, and check that the small-signal approximation is valid.
hints: DC first: I_D = (V_DD − 0.7)/R. Then r_d = nV_T/I_D.
In the small-signal circuit, v_d = v_s·r_d/(R + r_d).
checklist: Draw the ac equivalent and apply the divider.

questions.title: 8) Circuit Studio · Build and test a diode small-signal model
questions.promptHtml:
A small change around a DC bias point. Build a simple series circuit: a 5.00 V DC source, a 4.3 kΩ resistor, and a forward-biased diode. Connect the diode cathode (bar end) to ground and its anode to the resistor. Use the supplied diode model; for calculations use n = 1 and VT = 25.85 mV.

  1. Predict. Use VD ≈ 0.70 V to estimate IDQ = (5.00 − 0.70)/4300. Then calculate rd = nVT/IDQ. Sketch the incremental model with the diode replaced by rd.
  2. Build the schematic on the canvas and test it. The canvas contains only the unconnected voltage source, ground, R1 and diode. In Edit circuit, keep these four components and add the wires yourself. Wire V1+ → R1 → diode anode; connect the diode cathode and V1− to ground. Set V1 = 5.00 V and R1 = 4.3 kΩ; keep the supplied diode model (IS = 0.01 pA, n = 1). Run the DC test and record the diode voltage and current.
  3. Build the same circuit on the breadboard and test it. Open Build breadboard and place the components and jumpers yourself; Guide me and X-Ray are allowed. Check the wiring, then turn power on. Use the virtual multimeter with black on ground and red on the diode anode to measure VD,Q. Calculate IDQ = (5.00 − VD,Q)/4300. Compare with your canvas DC results.
  4. Test a small change. Recalculate rd from your measured bias current. Before changing the source, predict ΔID = 0.10/(4300 + rd) for a supply increase from 5.00 V to 5.10 V. Change the source to 5.10 V on the canvas and repeat its DC test. Verify that the breadboard source is also 5.10 V, recheck the wiring, and measure VD,2 on the breadboard. Calculate ID,2 = (5.10 − VD,2)/4300 and compare ID,2 − IDQ with your prediction. Keep all available voltage digits when calculating the currents.
  5. Explain and save. In one or two sentences, explain why rd describes small changes rather than the ratio VD,Q/IDQ. Capture your completed canvas schematic and breadboard. Record voltage and current at both supply settings for both the canvas and breadboard. Restore 5.00 V, save your progress, and reopen it to confirm your work is retained.

Use simulated supplies only. No capacitor, oscilloscope, or hidden-fault test is required.
hints: Use amperes in r_d = 0.02585/I_DQ; the result is in ohms.
The initial estimate is about 1 mA. The 0.10 V supply change is mostly across the 4.3 kΩ resistor.
Use the same diode model for both readings. Small differences from the hand estimate are expected.
checklist: Bias current and small-signal resistance predicted
Schematic constructed on the canvas and DC test completed
Readings at 5.00 V and 5.10 V recorded
Predicted and measured current changes compared
